**Summary.** This paper develops a nonperturbative semiclassical theory for magnetotransport in Weyl semimetals. It calculates the full magnetic field dependence of the conductivity tensor, demonstrating that conventional weak-field expansions are insufficient under certain conditions. The work provides exact closed-form expressions valid across various magnetic field regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter transport, the rigorous treatment of nonperturbative effects in response functions (like conductivity) using semiclassical methods shares conceptual overlap with analyzing quantum responses in open or driven systems where weak-field approximations fail.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a nonperturbative semiclassical theory for magnetotransport in Weyl semimetals, retaining the full magnetic-field dependence of conductivity.

**Main result.** The authors show that magnetotransport becomes intrinsically nonperturbative at low carrier densities or moderate fields, yielding closed-form expressions and revealing nonanalytic contributions absent in weak-field expansions.

**Method.** The study employs semiclassical chiral kinetic theory, deriving current density formulas by retaining the full magnetic field dependence of phase-space factors and generalized velocities.

**Model / system.** The system is Weyl semimetals, analyzed using a low-energy Hamiltonian near each Dirac node. The physics incorporates external electromagnetic fields ($\mathbf{E}, \mathbf{B}$) coupled to emergent chiral fields ($\mathbf{E}_\chi, \mathbf{B}_\chi$) and the orbital magnetic moment.

**Key observables.** The conductivity tensor components ($\sigma_{ij}$), particularly the intrinsic Hall response $\sigma_{Hall}^{\chi}(B)$, are key observables.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low carrier densities or moderate magnetic fields define the nonperturbative regime. The analysis is valid in the semiclassical limit, neglecting Landau quantization effects.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory relies on semiclassical approximations and assumes that retaining the full field dependence of the equations of motion captures physics beyond weak-field expansions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares exact nonperturbative results for $\sigma_{Hall}^{\chi}(B)$ against weak-field expansion predictions, showing deviations at moderate fields. Figure 2 illustrates Fermi-surface deformation induced by the orbital magnetic moment.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first establishing the semiclassical framework using effective chiral fields. It derives closed-form expressions for intrinsic currents and then analyzes conductivity components ($\sigma_{L}^{\perp}, \sigma_{L}^{H}, \sigma_{L}^{\parallel}$) by comparing results from full field dependence versus perturbative expansions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a nonperturbative semiclassical theory of magnetotransport in Weyl semimetals, retaining the full magnetic-field dependence of the Fermi-surface conductivity in the presence of Berry curvature and orbital magnetic moment effects. We obtain closed-form expressions valid to all orders in the magnetic field within the semiclassical regime. We show that the exact continuum formulation exhibits an intrinsic infrared sensitivity associated with the singular behavior of the orbital magnetic moment, requiring a physically motivated regularization. While the full conductivity tensor reduces to the standard quadratic magnetoconductivity, we demonstrate that magnetic-field expansion and momentum integration do not commute, leading to nonanalytic contributions at the level of scalar transport coefficients. Our results identify a regime, relevant for low carrier densities or moderate magnetic fields, where magnetotransport becomes intrinsically nonperturbative and cannot be captured by conventional weak-field expansions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores how itinerant electrons generate various forms of orbital magnetic ordering (ferro-, antiferro-, ferrimagnetic) on a honeycomb lattice. By decomposing the total magnetization into sublattice contributions, the authors map out distinct phases governed by model specifics and external potentials. This provides a detailed theoretical understanding of orbitally ordered states in condensed matter systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the rigorous decomposition of orbital response into symmetry-protected staggered/net components provides a powerful theoretical framework applicable to understanding emergent order parameters in complex quantum systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how itinerant orbital angular momentum can organize into magnetic patterns analogous to spin antiferromagnets, ferrimagnets, or ferromagnets.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate distinct regimes—orbital ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and ferrimagnetic states—by resolving the total orbital magnetization into sublattice contributions ($M_A$ and $M_B$).

**Method.** They employ real-space formulations and low-energy theory applied to a honeycomb lattice model, analyzing the system's response across varying parameters.

**Model / system.** The physical system is modeled using standard and modified Haldane tight-binding Hamiltonians on a honeycomb lattice. The analysis utilizes sublattice projection techniques to decompose the orbital magnetization into net ($M_z$) and staggered ($M_s^z$) components.

**Key observables.** Sublattice-resolved orbital magnetizations ($M_A, M_B$), total orbital magnetization ($M_z$), and staggered orbital magnetization ($M_s^z$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The sublattice potential ($\Delta$) and the Fermi energy are varied; specific results are highlighted for $\Delta=0$ and in insulating gap regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the itinerant orbital magnetization can be decomposed into contributions from different crystal sublattices, moving beyond localized moment descriptions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate electronic band gaps across parameter space ($\phi-\Delta$), and show sublattice-resolved DOS and orbital magnetizations for various regimes (e.g., $\Delta=0$ or in the insulating gap).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the Hamiltonian on a honeycomb lattice to calculating sublattice-resolved magnetization components, identifying distinct magnetic phases based on $M_z$ and $M_s^z$, and finally interpreting these results using low-energy valley mechanisms.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Because electronic orbital angular momentum in solids is inherently non-local, its contribution to magnetism is usually cast in terms of a net orbital magnetization. Here, we show that itinerant electrons can generate orbital magnetic phases with ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or ferrimagnetic orders. We demonstrate this possibility in a honeycomb lattice, using both the standard and a modified Haldane model. Employing real-space formulations, we decompose the itinerant orbital magnetization into sublattice contributions, $M_A$ and $M_B$. Their net ($M_z=M_A+M_B$) and staggered ($M_z^s=M_A-M_B$) combinations are then used to identify the orbital order. By varying the sublattice potential and the Fermi energy, we find distinct regimes: a (PT)-symmetric orbital antiferromagnet in the modified Haldane model, an orbital ferromagnet in the standard Haldane model, ferrimagnetic metallic states where net and staggered orbital magnetizations coexist, and insulating regimes in which the ferro- and antiferromagnetic orbital characters can be interchanged.These findings are explained by a low-energy theory in terms of two distinct valley mechanisms: valley-dependent Dirac masses in the standard Haldane model and valley-dependent energy shifts in its modified version.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates evidence for 'spin swapping' in magnetic heterostructures by measuring how transverse resistance changes with an out-of-plane magnetic field. The key finding is that opposite signs of the measured resistance modulation correspond to the opposite spin chirality of the Rashba interfaces, supporting a model where spin current direction swaps within the non-magnetic spacer layer.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on spintronics/condensed matter magnetism, the clear dependence of macroscopic transport properties ($\Delta R_{xy}$) on microscopic symmetry breaking (Rashba interface chirality) provides a tangible experimental test case for complex quantum mechanical spin-orbit coupling effects.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates evidence for a physical phenomenon called 'spin swapping' by analyzing how the transverse resistance of magnetic heterostructures changes when subjected to an out-of-plane magnetic field.

**Main result.** Opposite modulations in the transverse resistance ($\Delta R_{xy}$) observed between two different Rashba interfaces (Cu/Bi2O3 vs Ag/Bi2O3) correlate with opposite spin chiralities, suggesting that spin swapping is responsible for generating a transverse spin current with opposing flow directions.

**Method.** The researchers measured the transverse resistance ($R_{xy}$) as a function of an out-of-plane magnetic field ($\mathbf{H}$), calculating $\Delta R_{xy} = R_{xy}(+\mathbf{H}) - R_{xy}(-\mathbf{H})$ to diagnose the spin transport mechanism.

**Model / system.** The experiment uses magnetic heterostructures, specifically Py/Cu(or Ag)/Bi2O3, where the Cu or Ag layers act as Rashba interfaces with opposite spin chiralities. The physics is analyzed through the lens of spin-charge conversion and subsequent spin current dynamics.

**Key observables.** Transverse resistance modulation ($\Delta R_{xy}$), anomalous Hall angle ($	heta_{AH}^{	ext{add}}$), and their dependence on non-magnetic metal (NM) thickness ($t_{	ext{NM}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Out-of-plane magnetic field ($\mathbf{H}$), Rashba interface chirality, and the thickness of the non-magnetic spacer layer ($t_{	ext{NM}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The spin swapping effect is hypothesized to occur primarily near the ferromagnetic (FM) layer, and intermixing between FM and NM layers is acknowledged as a potential contributing factor.

**Figures summary.** Figures 1(b) and 1(c) show $R_{xy}$ vs $\mathbf{H}$ demonstrating opposite modulation signs for the two interfaces. Figure 2 shows $	heta_{AH}$ dependence on $t_{	ext{NM}}$, while Figure 3 displays the interface-added contribution ($	heta_{AH}^{	ext{add}}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the transverse resistance response using magnetic field sweeps and thickness variations, correlating the observed sign changes in transport measurements with theoretical predictions derived from spin chirality differences.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the transverse response under the out-of-plane magnetic field for magnetic heterostructures with Cu/Bi2O3 or Ag/Bi2O3 Rashba interfaces. We detect opposite contributions on the transverse resistance by the Cu/Bi2O3 and the Ag/Bi2O3 interfaces, which interestingly coincide well with the opposite signs of the spin/charge interconversion from the two interfaces. We suppose the opposite influences on the transverse resistance feature spin swapping occurrence of the converted spin current. The transverse spin flow emerges due to the spin swapping in both Cu and Ag layer, but the direction of the spin flow is opposed dependent on the spin direction of the converted spin current.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work investigates superconducting pairing symmetry in La3Ni2O7 by incorporating strong electronic correlations using DMFT within an RPA framework. The key finding is that these correlation effects fundamentally change the predicted gap symmetry, stabilizing a sign-changing s+ state over the dxy state favored by simpler models. This highlights the necessity of treating quasiparticle renormalization for accurate predictions in correlated superconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on cuprate/nickelate physics, the methodology—using DMFT to correct RPA susceptibilities for strong correlations—is a general technique applicable to understanding unconventional superconductivity in any strongly correlated material system.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The superconducting gap symmetry of pressurized La3Ni2O7 is unsettled due to competition between sign-changing s-wave and d-wave instabilities predicted by weak-coupling theories.

**Main result.** Including strong correlation effects via DMFT renormalizes the pairing instability, reversing the leading symmetry from a B2g dxy state (in bare RPA) to an A1g sign-changing s+ state.

**Method.** The study combines single-site two-orbital Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) with a self-energy-renormalized Random-Phase Approximation (RPA).

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using a four-orbital Wannier Hamiltonian for pressurized La3Ni2O7, focusing on the interplay between orbital degrees of freedom and electronic correlations.

**Key observables.** Superconducting pairing symmetry ($	ext{A}_{1g}$ $s_{\pm}$, $	ext{B}_{2g}$ $d_{xy}$), static spin susceptibility, and quasiparticle weights ($Z$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The inclusion of the DMFT self-energy is the crucial parameter change compared to bare RPA calculations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that strong correlations are not a secondary correction but fundamentally alter the pairing mechanism by renormalizing quasiparticles.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the leading pairing eigenvalues between ordinary RPA and DMFT-dressed RPA, showing the symmetry reversal from $d_{xy}$ to $s_{\pm}$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem using weak-coupling theory (RPA benchmark), then introduces the correlated treatment by replacing the bare bubble with a DMFT-derived one. It analyzes the resulting pairing hierarchy and validates the findings using spin susceptibility calculations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The superconducting gap symmetry of pressurized La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ remains unsettled because conventional weak-coupling calculations often place the system close to competing sign-changing $s$- and $d$-wave instabilities. Using the four-orbital Wannier Hamiltonian of Xia et al., we combine single-site two-orbital dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) with a self-energy-renormalized random-phase approximation (RPA). The central step is to replace the bare particle-hole bubble $G_0G_0$ of ordinary RPA by a $G_{\rm DMFT}G_{\rm DMFT}$ bubble, while keeping the same residual Slater--Kanamori interaction vertices. In the bare RPA benchmark, the leading pairing eigenvalue belongs to the $B_{2g}$ $d_{xy}$ channel. Once the DMFT self-energy is included, the hierarchy is reversed: the $A_{1g}$ sign-changing $s_{\pm}$ state becomes dominant, the $B_{1g}$ $d_{x^2-y^2}$ channel is subleading, and the original $B_{2g}$ instability is strongly suppressed. Pocket-pair decomposition and orbital-resolved susceptibilities show that the reversal originates from orbital-selective renormalization of the $d_{3z^2-r^2}$ sector, which filters the $γ$-pocket scattering processes that stabilize $d_{xy}$ pairing in bare RPA while preserving distributed inter-pocket processes favorable to $s_{\pm}$ pairing. As an independent two-particle validation, we further compute the static spin susceptibility using the dual Bethe--Salpeter equation with the local DMFT vertex. The resulting susceptibility retains a broad finite-momentum magnetic response and is weak near $Γ$, strengthening the spin-fluctuation background for the correlation-stabilized $s_{\pm}$ state. Our results demonstrate that strong correlations are not a secondary correction in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$: an appropriate treatment of correlation-renormalized quasiparticles is essential for predicting the superconducting pairing symmetry.

</details>

**Summary.** This work theoretically examines how superconductivity emerges in bilayer heterostructures as a function of layer mass contrast. By applying Eliashberg theory, the authors demonstrate a continuous crossover from plasmon-mediated pairing (low mass ratio) to phonon-like pairing (high mass ratio). The study suggests that SC might be robustly present across this entire parameter space.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on superconductivity mechanisms, the systematic theoretical framework for analyzing pairing mediated by collective excitations (plasmons vs. phonons) in layered systems is relevant to understanding strongly correlated electron physics and emergent quantum phenomena.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the mechanism of superconductivity in bilayer van der Waals heterostructures, specifically tracking the crossover from acoustic plasmon-mediated pairing to acoustic phonon-mediated pairing.

**Main result.** Superconductivity is predicted to exist continuously as the mass ratio between the two layers ($m_2/m_1$) is tuned, suggesting that SC may be a generic feature in bilayers with large mass differences.

**Method.** The analysis employs Eliashberg theory combined with calculations of the dynamically screened Coulomb interaction derived within the Random Phase Approximation (RPA).

**Model / system.** The model consists of a bilayer system comprising two 2D electron gases: a light layer (LL) and a heavy layer (HL), whose coupling mediates the pairing interaction.

**Key observables.** Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), which is studied as a function of various physical parameters.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The mass ratio ($m_2/m_1$) is the primary tuning parameter, alongside carrier densities and an artificial frequency cut-off ($\omega_c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key approximations include using RPA for screening and introducing a frequency cut-off ($\omega_c$) to handle divergences in Eliashberg theory.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dependence of $\log_{10}(T_c)$ on density and mass ratio, showing trends across different fixed values of the frequency cut-off.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the pairing interaction derived from acoustic plasmons using RPA, applies this to the linearized Eliashberg equation, and then maps out the continuous crossover behavior by varying the layer mass ratio $m_2/m_1$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Motivated by recent developments in van der Waals heterostructures, we revisit the acoustic plasmon mechanism of superconductivity in bilayer systems composed of a light layer (LL) and heavy layer (HL) by employing Eliashberg theory. The exchange of virtual plasmons in the HL can lead to a retarded in time attractive interaction between electrons of LL that we model through the screened interaction in the bilayer system within the random phase approximation. We explore the evolution from acoustic plasmon mediated superconductivity to phonon mediated superconductivity by studying the evolution of $T_c$ as the HL mass is increased by a few orders of magnitude compared with the electronic mass in LL. The lower HL mass corresponds to the bilayer acoustic plasmon, while the latter regime is closer to the Born-Oppenheimer regime of acoustic phonon mediated strongly retarded pairing. The heavy HL mass limit is known to obey Migdal's theorem by virtue of the small ratio of the two individual layer masses. We study the nonadiabatic effects for the arbitrary mass ratio with no small parameter systematically by using a frequency cut off in the Eliashberg theory, providing $T_c$ as a function of this cut off.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper constructs a 'quantum membrane paradigm' for black hole horizons by modeling them using matrix quantum mechanics. It shows that the horizon dynamics are governed by Lowest-Landau-Level (LLL) states on a fuzzy sphere, which generate measurable electric currents. This microscopic description provides a physical origin for boundary conditions previously treated classically.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on gravity, the use of LLL states, topological structures (Berry monopole), and emergent current generation from fundamental degrees of freedom shares conceptual overlap with strongly correlated electron systems and quantum Hall physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a microscopic quantum membrane paradigm for black hole horizons by providing a physical origin for boundary conditions typically used in classical descriptions.

**Main result.** The construction replaces the fictitious classical membrane with a dynamical quantum membrane populated by LLL degrees of freedom, yielding explicit quantum corrections to horizon boundary conditions.

**Method.** The authors use matrix quantum mechanics models involving fuzzy spheres and Fermi seas to derive effective field theories for the horizon dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system models quantum black holes using a matrix quantum mechanics framework equivalent to a fuzzy sphere coupled with a half-filled sea of 'horizon partons.'

**Key observables.** Ohmic, Hall, and polarization currents on the horizon; generalized boundary conditions for external electromagnetic fields.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The rank $N$ of the matrix model ($N=2J+1$) determines the monopole charge $c_1 = N-1$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mapping the system to a matrix quantum mechanics description and utilizing large-$N$ limits.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by notes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the fuzzy sphere/Fermi sea structure, deriving the Berry monopole, analyzing LLL dynamics leading to transport currents, and finally introducing link variables whose condensation locks the horizon gauge field to external fields.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a microscopic quantum membrane paradigm from the matrix quantum mechanics of black holes [1]. It was proposed that a quantum black hole is described by a fuzzy sphere together with a half-filled Fermi sea of horizon partons. We show that the topology of the fuzzy sphere induces a Berry monopole, providing a microscopic origin for the monopole appearing in the tunneling description of the decay of quantum black hole. Because the partons couple to the fuzzy sphere as fundamental degrees of freedom, they are sensitive to this monopole and form Lowest-Landau-Level (LLL) states rather than ordinary propagating two-dimensional fermions. Their guiding-center dynamics generates Ohmic, Hall, and polarization currents on the horizon. To couple these currents to an external electromagnetic field, we introduce a two-block matrix configuration comprising black-hole, environmental, and bifundamental link sectors. Off-diagonal link modes become tachyonic near the fuzzy sphere and condense, dynamically locking the horizon gauge field to the boundary value of the external Maxwell field. The parton current thereby becomes a physical boundary source for the exterior field. Our construction replaces the fictitious membrane of the classical paradigm with a dynamical quantum membrane populated by microscopic LLL degrees of freedom. The resulting boundary condition generalizes the classical ingoing membrane condition and yields explicit quantum, frequency-dependent, and helicity-dependent corrections, offering a possible probe of the microscopic quantum structure of the horizon.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper microscopically investigates the critical current for vortex entry in a superconducting thin film strip. By analyzing the stability of the zero-vortex state using advanced Usadel theory, the authors demonstrate that this threshold current precisely matches the depairing current under ideal conditions. This provides a rigorous, microscopic confirmation of established superconducting critical current concepts.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous application of stability analysis (saddle-node bifurcation) using functional methods is relevant to understanding phase transitions or instability thresholds in complex quantum systems beyond standard BCS theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work aims to microscopically determine the current density at which magnetic vortices enter a superconducting thin-film strip ($J_v$) and compare this value against the depairing current ($J_{dp}$).

**Main result.** For an ideal homogeneous zero-field strip, the microscopic stability analysis shows that the vortex-entry current is exactly equal to the depairing current ($J_v = J_{dp}$).

**Method.** The problem is formulated by analyzing the stability of the vortex-free state using the fixed-current Gibbs functional derived from dirty-limit Usadel theory, examining both uniform and nonuniform perturbations.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a homogeneous superconducting thin-film strip assumed to be infinite in one direction and analyzed at zero applied magnetic field. The theoretical framework relies on the fixed-current Gibbs functional of dirty-limit Usadel theory.

**Key observables.** Vortex-entry current density ($J_v$), depairing current density ($J_{dp}$), and the stability criterion derived from minimizing the quadratic energy cost ($\delta^2 G$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$) relative to $T_c$, applied current density ($J$), and dimensionless parameters related to gauge-invariant momentum ($Q$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes an ideal, homogeneous strip geometry and neglects magnetic self-field effects for the primary calculation.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by reformulating the vortex entry problem as a local stability analysis of the current-carrying state. It first examines uniform perturbations to find a candidate critical current, and then rigorously proves that nonuniform modes do not destabilize the system at lower currents than the uniform mode.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The current at which vortices enter a superconducting strip is usually identified in Pearl--London theory with the disappearance of an edge barrier. This work reformulates the same question microscopically as the loss of local stability of the vortex-free current-carrying state, using the fixed-current Gibbs functional of dirty-limit Usadel theory, which is valid at arbitrary temperatures. For an ideal homogeneous thin-film strip at zero applied field, with self-field effects neglected, the stability of the vortex-free state is examined against both spatially uniform and nonuniform perturbations. The barrier-disappearance current is shown to be set by the uniform perturbation and to coincide exactly with the depairing current.

</details>

**Summary.** This research details the development of $	ext{NaBiF}_4:	ext{Er}^{3+}, 	ext{Yb}^{3+}$ upconversion particles as advanced bio-markers. The authors demonstrate that these particles exhibit superior optical properties compared to their Yttrium counterparts, coupled with surface chemistry enabling biocompatibility. Crucially, they establish protocols to actively control the particle's luminescence signal using two distinct near-infrared laser wavelengths.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work involves complex non-linear optical processes (upconversion, stimulated emission depletion) in solid-state materials, which touches upon open quantum systems dynamics and energy transfer mechanisms relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is achieving high-contrast, sub-diffraction bioimaging using upconversion particles without requiring high-power lasers in noisy biological media.

**Main result.** Bismuth-doped UCPs ($	ext{NaBiF}_4:	ext{Er}^{3+}, 	ext{Yb}^{3+}$) are shown to be superior biomarkers due to enhanced quantum yield and the ability to achieve controllable PL quenching/enhancement via dual-wavelength excitation.

**Method.** The study combines optical characterization (PL spectroscopy, time-resolved measurements), physical modification (sol-gel coating, APTES functionalization), and modeling of energy transfer dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system is based on lanthanide-doped upconversion particles ($	ext{NaBiF}_4$) excited by near-infrared lasers ($975 	ext{ nm}$ and $1064 	ext{ nm}$). The PL dynamics are modeled using a simplified stimulated emission depletion process involving three energy levels.

**Key observables.** Quantum yield (3x overall, 4x red), systematic quenching/enhancement of PL by adjusting laser power, optical trapping stiffness ($\kappa$), and characteristic fluorescence lifetimes ($	au_1, 	au_2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Near-infrared excitation wavelengths ($975 	ext{ nm}, 1064 	ext{ nm}$), sub-diffraction particle thickness ($\sim 100 	ext{ nm}$), and the relative powers of the two exciting lasers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The PL dynamics are modeled as a simplified stimulated emission depletion process, and the initial studies on quenching/enhancement protocols are presented as proof-of-concept.

**Figures summary.** Figures show SEM images comparing particle morphology; FTIR spectra confirm successful silica coating and amino functionalization; PL spectra compare $	ext{NaBiF}$ vs. $	ext{NaYF}$; and other figures detail the dependence of fluorescence lifetimes on laser powers and temperature.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical superiority of $	ext{NaBiF}_4$ over $	ext{NaYF}$ (enhanced quantum yield) to demonstrating its multi-functionality: surface modification for biocompatibility, optical trapping capability, and finally, detailed control over PL emission via dual-wavelength excitation protocols.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Lanthanide-doped upconversion particles (UCPs) have revolutionized optical bioimaging platforms because of their excellent photostability, non-toxicity, and utilization of near-infrared excitation, which facilitates deep tissue penetration with negligible autofluorescence. However, it remains a challenge to achieve high-contrast and sub-diffraction imaging in noisy biological media, without using a high-power laser. Here, we report various protocols applied to bismuth-doped UCPs address some of these challenges. Compared to the photoluminescence (PL) emission of the regular Yttrium doped UCPs, we observe a three-fold increment in the quantum yield of the overall emission of bismuth-UCPs, and a four-fold increment, specifically, in red emission. Leveraging this advantage, we devise a protocol employing two infrared wavelengths, 975 nm and 1064 nm, to selectively control the PL emission. Interestingly, our results reveal two distinct regimes in which PL can be systematically quenched or enhanced, by adjusting the 975 nm laser power. We model the overall dynamics as a simplified stimulated emission depletion process involving three energy levels. In addition, the particle has a thickness under sub-diffraction, shows optical trapping ability, and potential of surface functionalization to enable specific conjugation with diverse biospecimens. These studies establish bismuth doped UCPs as an excellent candidate in accomplishing advanced biomarker operating with enhanced signal-to-noise ratio and sub-diffraction imaging capabilities.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes how fluctuations above the critical temperature ($T_c$) induce nonreciprocal electrical responses like dichroism and gyrotropy in 2D noncentrosymmetric superconductors. Using generalized Ginzburg-Landau theory, the authors show these effects critically depend on particle-hole asymmetry and require broken inversion/time-reversal symmetry. The results offer a pathway to probe superconducting dynamics using techniques like quantum noise spectroscopy.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit derivation of nonreciprocal responses from fluctuation effects provides a concrete theoretical link between broken symmetries (inversion/time-reversal) and measurable optical properties in superconductors, relevant to understanding exotic quantum states.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how superconducting fluctuations induce nonreciprocal dichroism and gyrotropy in two-dimensional, noncentrosymmetric superconductors.

**Main result.** These nonreciprocal effects require the simultaneous breaking of inversion and time-reversal symmetries and are dependent on particle-hole asymmetry. The reactive component (birefringence) shows a critical enhancement as temperature approaches $T_c$.

**Method.** The authors utilize time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, calculating the Aslamazov-Larkin contribution to the gyrotropic conductivity in closed form.

**Model / system.** The model is a two-dimensional noncentrosymmetric superconductor, exemplified by gated transition metal dichalcogenides like $	ext{MoS}_2$. The theory incorporates particle-hole asymmetry and the cubic Lifshitz invariant of trigonal superconductors.

**Key observables.** Nonreciprocal conductivity (dichroism and gyrotropy), which are analyzed via even-in-$k$ ($\sigma_{	ext{even}}$) and odd-in-$k$ ($\sigma_{	ext{odd}}$) components.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature relative to $T_c$, particle-hole asymmetry parameter ($\gamma_2$), and the frequency $\omega$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that nonreciprocal terms do not alter the leading order results for gyrotropy near $T_c$ (Appendix B).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the frequency dependence of the derived fluctuation conductivity, showing distinct behaviors for the dissipative dichroism ($W(\varpi)$) and reactive birefringence ($V(\varpi)$).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first establishing the theoretical framework using TDGL theory, then calculating the $	ext{AL}$ contribution to gyrotropy, analyzing the symmetry dependence on particle-hole asymmetry ($\gamma_2$), and finally discussing experimental implications for probing superconducting dynamics.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the spatially dispersive conductivity of a two-dimensional noncentrosymmetric superconductor, demonstrating that it acquires a nonreciprocal, odd-in-wavevector component from fluctuation-induced Cooper pairs above the critical temperature $T_c$. Utilizing time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory generalized to include particle-hole asymmetry and the cubic Lifshitz invariant of trigonal superconductors, we compute the Aslamazov-Larkin contribution to the gyrotropic conductivity in closed form, including its complete frequency dependence. The dissipative part describes nonreciprocal directional dichroism: it is odd in frequency and displays a nonmonotonic dependence, peaking at frequencies comparable to the decay rate of fluctuating Cooper pairs. Its Kramers-Kronig dual component describes gyrotropic birefringence, which remains finite in the static limit and is strongly enhanced as the temperature approaches $T_c$. Both effects require simultaneously broken inversion and time-reversal symmetries, are dependent on particle-hole asymmetry in close analogy to the fluctuation Hall effect, and trace to the same asymmetric Cooper-pair dispersion responsible for the superconducting diode effect and the giant magnetochiral anisotropy observed near $T_c$. This critical enhancement dominates over the smooth normal-state gyrotropy, which we evaluate for the same band model as a baseline. Finally, we frame our analysis within the context of gated transition metal dichalcogenides like MoS$_2$, discussing the implications for probing superconducting dynamics through nitrogen-vacancy-center quantum noise spectroscopy.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a powerful theoretical framework to analyze how axion topological insulators respond to external electric and magnetic fields. By reformulating the problem using 'surface variables' instead of bulk descriptions, the authors derive solvable integral equations for induced surface charges and currents. This method allows for detailed numerical simulations on complex geometries like spheres and tori.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly focused on quantum information, the rigorous mathematical treatment of topological responses using reduced-dimensionality surface variable methods is highly relevant to modern condensed matter theory dealing with emergent electromagnetic properties in novel materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on determining the macroscopic quasi-static magnetoelectric response of axion topological materials, specifically topological insulators, when subjected to external static electric and magnetic fields.

**Main result.** The authors derive a set of integral equations governing effective surface charge and current densities, providing exact analytic solutions for axial-symmetric cases and developing a boundary finite element method for complex geometries.

**Method.** The core methodology involves reformulating the bulk field equations using 'surface variables' (effective surface charge/current), leading to linear integral equations that are solved numerically via a boundary finite element approach.

**Model / system.** The system is an axion topological material characterized by a sharp discontinuity in the axion field ($	heta$). The physics is governed by modified Maxwell's equations incorporating induced sources derived from $
abla	heta$, leading to integral equations for surface variables.

**Key observables.** Effective surface charge density ($\omega_s$) and surface current density ($s_s$), as well as the resulting electric and magnetic fields.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Quasi-static regime, external static E and B fields, geometry (spheres, tori).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a quasi-static limit and treats $
abla	heta$ as localized at material interfaces, allowing the problem to be reduced to surface integral equations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the calculated field distributions (E and B) and induced charges/currents for various geometries like tori and hollow spheres under external fields or point charges.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a logical progression: establishing the Hamiltonian formulation, introducing surface variables to derive integral equations, presenting analytic solutions for simple cases, detailing the numerical boundary finite element method, and finally applying this framework to complex geometries.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the response of axion topological materials under the presence of external static electric and magnetic fields. We focus on the macroscopic quasi-static magnetoelectric response of topological insulators. We use techniques based on surface variables that have been previously employed in soft condensed matter problems for the description of heterogeneous systems composed of multiple homogeneous materials. A complete description of the whole system is written in terms of surface degrees of freedom, which in this case correspond to effective surface charge and surface current densities. We obtain a set of integral equations satisfied by these variables. We present exact analytic solutions for axial-symmetric cases. We develop a numerical method for the solution of the integral equations by means of a boundary finite element method. We apply the numerical method to topological insulators with different geometries such as spheres, hollow spheres and toroidal surfaces. We show that that a variational principle can be used to recover the surface variables equations.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work develops a minimal, symmetry-constrained model for describing Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs in the topological semimetal $	ext{PtBi}_2$. By incorporating spin-orbit coupling terms derived from DFT, the authors successfully predict how these nodes split and annihilate. The resulting Hamiltonian provides a robust starting point for understanding surface superconductivity mechanisms in such materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on topological materials physics rather than AMO systems, the rigorous use of symmetry constraints to build an effective Hamiltonian from first principles is highly relevant. The techniques for analyzing band topology and emergent symmetries are transferable to understanding exotic phases in quantum simulators or superconducting qubits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work aims to develop a minimal, symmetry-constrained theoretical model for understanding the topological electronic features—Weyl nodes and Fermi arcs—in the Weyl semimetal $	ext{PtBi}_2$. This bridges the gap between complex *ab initio* calculations and simplified effective descriptions.

**Main result.** A minimal Hamiltonian was constructed that successfully reproduces the topology, captures the spin-orbit coupling (SOC)-driven splitting, and models the subsequent annihilation of Weyl nodes in momentum space. The model also describes the characteristic spin-momentum locking on surface Fermi arcs.

**Method.** The methodology combines symmetry analysis (using tools like qsymm) with continuum Hamiltonian construction, guided by DFT results to constrain low-energy band physics.

**Model / system.** The system is trigonal $	ext{PtBi}_2$, modeled using a tight-binding approach incorporating orbital degrees of freedom ($\{p_x, p_y\}$) and SOC terms. The Hamiltonian is built sector-by-sector to enforce crystal symmetries ($C_{3v}$) across multiple coupled blocks.

**Key observables.** Weyl node chirality ($\chi$), Fermi arc spin texture (spin polarization $\langle S_z angle/ho$), and the evolution of nodes/arcs as a function of SOC coupling strength ($\lambda$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** SOC couplings ($g_1, g_2$, etc.), critical coupling strengths ($g_c$) for node annihilation, and momentum-dependent terms derived from DFT.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes that the low-energy physics is dominated by specific orbital components ($	ext{Bi } 6p$ orbitals) and that the Hamiltonian can be effectively described by a minimal set of symmetry-allowed terms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate band structures near Weyl nodes, map the twelve Weyl points in the Brillouin zone under $C_{3v}$ symmetry, and show the evolution of node trajectories as SOC strength increases. Surface density of states plots confirm the presence and spin texture of Fermi arcs.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing a basic model constrained by symmetries to incorporating SOC terms that cause node splitting and annihilation. It then extends this description to incorporate full $C_{3v}$ symmetry via multi-sector coupling, culminating in a detailed analysis of how different SOC components affect spin texture and nodal structure.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Weyl semimetals host topologically protected Fermi arcs on their surfaces, originating from the Chern number of the bulk Weyl nodes. In trigonal PtBi$_2$, superconducting signatures have been associated with the Fermi arcs. Theoretical descriptions of this surface superconductivity have so far relied on effective models that are not directly tied to the microscopic electronic structure of the material. In this work we develop a minimal description of the low-energy bands guided by density functional theory calculations and fully constrained by the relevant crystalline and time-reversal symmetries. The model captures the evolution of the Weyl nodes with spin-orbit coupling, including node annihilations, and is able to describe the spin-momentum locking of the surface Fermi arcs. It reproduces the orbital content and the band topology of PtBi$_2$ and provides a starting point for further studies.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes Akhmediev breathers in the Manakov system, challenging the assumption that breather spectra must be governed by linearly unstable modes. Through numerical simulation and detailed analysis of nonlinear forcing, the authors prove that a spectrally stable harmonic can spontaneously become dominant at the breather's peak. This mechanism is driven purely by four-wave mixing, offering new insights into nonlinear wave dynamics across various physical platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete example of how strong nonlinearity can fundamentally alter the spectral dynamics of wave packets, suggesting that energy transfer mechanisms (like four-wave mixing) can overcome linear stability constraints in physical systems relevant to quantum optics and Bose-Einstein condensates.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether an Akhmediev breather (AB) can be spectrally dominated by a frequency component that is linearly stable, contrary to the usual expectation derived from modulation instability theory.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that in the Manakov system, a stable harmonic component ($n=\pm 2$) can spontaneously emerge and dominate the spectrum of an AB peak, driven entirely by four-wave mixing from initially unstable modes.

**Method.** The analysis combines linear stability theory (calculating MI gain) with numerical simulations using the Manakov equation to track spectral energy distribution over time.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by the Manakov nonlinear Schrödinger equation, governing two coupled wave components ($\psi^{(1)}, \psi^{(2)}$). The analysis focuses on constructing and simulating a third-order Akhmediev breather solution.

**Key observables.** Dominance measure $D(j)$ (quantifying stable harmonic contribution), Fourier amplitudes $|A_n|$, and the nonlinear forcing term derived from four-wave mixing.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The wavenumber offset $eta$ is critical, with a specific window ($1 \le eta < 1.5$) identified where this spectral dominance occurs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of the Manakov system description and relies on isolating the nonlinear forcing term to quantify its source (four-wave mixing).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the transition of the dominance measure $D(j)$ towards unity for specific parameters, show the time evolution of Fourier amplitudes peaking at stable harmonics, and confirm that four-wave mixing accounts for most of the nonlinear driving.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical conflict (stable vs. unstable spectral control) to constructing the AB solution, performing linear stability analysis, running numerical simulations on the Manakov system, and finally quantifying the mechanism via nonlinear forcing analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the scalar nonlinear Schrodinger equation, an Akhmediev breather (AB) is dominated by a frequency that lies inside the modulation instability gain band. This exactly correspondence between instability and breathers is challenged in vector systems such as the Manakov system, where the gain spectrum splits into disconnected lobes separated by stable gaps. We analytically and numerically construct an AB that is generated by unstable modes but is spectrally dominated by a stable harmonic at its peak. Numerical simulations starting from a simple continuous wave background perturbed only by the unstable harmonics confirm that the stable component emerges spontaneously and becomes dominant without any initial seed. We identify the precise parameter window in which this phenomenon occurs and show that this passive amplification of the linearly stable component is driven by four-wave mixing, which accounts for 96% of the nonlinear forcing. Given the universality of the Manakov system across nonlinear physics, from nonlinear optics to ultracold quantum gases, these results open an experimentally accessible new perspective on breather dynamics, one in which linearly stable frequencies can dominate.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops an extension of Lifshitz-Kosevich theory to describe quantum oscillations arising from anomalous Landau levels found in topological flat bands. By analyzing the temperature dependence of these oscillations, the authors demonstrate that the thermal damping factor yields a measurable effective mass directly proportional to the system's underlying quantum geometric structure.

**Why it may be interesting.** The direct link established between measurable transport properties (thermal damping of oscillations) and fundamental geometric invariants (the quantum metric) provides a powerful new experimental probe for characterizing topological band structures in condensed matter systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine how quantum oscillations persist in topological flat bands, which naively suggest thermal suppression due to zero group velocity, and whether the thermal damping factor can reveal information about the underlying quantum geometry.

**Main result.** The paper derives an LK theory for anomalous Landau levels (ALLs), showing that their persistent oscillations yield a finite, field-dependent effective mass whose thermal damping directly measures the quantum metric of the flat band.

**Method.** The authors adapt the Lifshitz-Kosevich formalism to analyze the grand potential and magnetization oscillations in the presence of an anomalous LL spacing. They fit temperature dependence using standard LK forms to extract effective masses.

**Model / system.** The study uses a minimal model Hamiltonian describing topological flat bands, relevant to moiré materials, which possess Time-Reversal and inversion symmetries. The analysis is performed under a perpendicular magnetic field at fixed carrier density.

**Key observables.** Magnetization ($M$) oscillations as a function of $1/B$, the extracted effective mass ($m^*_{	ext{eff}}$), and the thermal damping factor derived from the fundamental harmonic amplitude ($A_1(T)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Magnetic field ($B$), temperature ($T$), carrier density ($ho$), and parameters related to the quantum metric tensor.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on a minimal model with perfectly flat topological bands, and it treats the local LK fit as a diagnostic tool for measuring the effective mass derived from thermal damping.

**Figures summary.** Figures show band dispersion, Berry curvature distribution, LL spectra, and magnetization oscillations ($M$ vs $1/B$) for both normal and anomalous LLs. Subsequent figures compare extracted effective masses against analytical expectations.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem by contrasting conventional Landau quantization with flat bands. It then adapts the LK formalism to derive oscillatory terms ($\delta\Omega$), analyzes the thermal damping factor ($R_T(p)$), and finally extracts the field-dependent effective mass, linking it theoretically to the quantum metric.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In conventional metals, quantum oscillations arise from Landau quantization of Fermi-surface cyclotron orbits, whose dynamics are governed by the Fermi velocity and cyclotron effective mass within Lifshitz-Kosevich (LK) theory. A perfectly flat band, by contrast, has vanishing group velocity, which would naively imply an infinite cyclotron mass and complete thermal suppression of quantum oscillations. Yet topological flat bands can support anomalous Landau levels (LLs) whose finite-field spacing is generated by quantum geometry rather than band curvature, allowing quantum oscillations to persist. This work addresses how such anomalous flat-band LLs behave within the LK framework and whether their thermal damping can reveal quantum geometric information. Using a minimal model with exactly flat topological bands, we derive an LK theory for these anomalous LLs and analyze fixed-density magnetization oscillations. The resulting oscillations exhibit a finite LK effective mass that is substantially larger than the normal-band value and possesses a strong magnetic-field dependence. In the weak-field limit, this anomalous mass reflects the quantum geometric origin of the LL spacing and scales inversely with both the magnetic field and the trace of the quantum metric. Thus, thermal damping of flat-band quantum oscillations directly measures the quantum metric, establishing quantum oscillations as a probe to flat-band quantum geometry.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates friction at nanoscale contacts using crystalline SiO2/SiO2 interfaces. It develops a modified continuum model that integrates atomistic simulation results for shear strength and adhesion effects. The resulting framework successfully predicts experimental observations, particularly the stiffness collapse during sliding, demonstrating its relevance to realistic micro-tribology.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid mechanics and tribology, the development of a multiscale constitutive model that accurately captures transition regimes (stick-slip) by incorporating non-linear material properties (adhesion, load dependence) is relevant to understanding complex boundary conditions in quantum systems or interfaces where classical assumptions break down.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work aims to bridge the theoretical understanding of superlubricity at atomically flat interfaces with the reality of tribological systems governed by Hertzian contact geometry.

**Main result.** A modified Mindlin model, incorporating load-dependent shear strength and adhesion, successfully reproduces key experimental signatures like stiffness collapse in oscillatory shear tests on passivated contacts.

**Method.** The study combines atomistic simulations (calculating Interfacial Sliding Potential Energy Surfaces) with the extension of classical continuum mechanics models (Mindlin's model).

**Model / system.** The system studied is the friction and sliding behavior at crystalline SiO2/SiO2 interfaces. The theoretical framework uses a modified Mindlin model to account for non-uniform Hertzian stress distributions, adhesion, and load dependence.

**Key observables.** Load-dependent shear strength ($	au$), Minimal-Scale Sliding (MSS) friction ($\sigma$), effective lateral stiffness ($k$), and total lateral force ($Q$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Normal pressure ($P$) up to 3 GPa, the adhesion-limited intercept ($	au_0$), and the critical radius defining stick/slip zones.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The simulation assumes an atomically flat profile is maintained; the model extends classical frameworks by incorporating finite adhesion and load dependence, which are crucial for matching experimental results.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the constant-pressure ISPES showing minimum energy pathways, radial distributions of shear stress vs. applied stress (Figure 4), and oscillatory shear response comparing bare vs. graphene-passivated contacts showing stiffness collapse (Figure 6).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for a multiscale approach by simulating ISPES to find load-dependent friction parameters ($	au, \sigma$). It then extends the Mindlin model using these parameters to predict behavior under Hertzian loading. Finally, it validates this modified model against oscillatory shear experiments.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding friction at single-asperity contacts is essential for bridging the gap between nanoscale structural superlubricity and realistic tribological systems dominated by Hertzian contact geometry. In this work, we combine atomistic simulations and a modified continuum model to investigate the onset of sliding at crystalline SiO$_2$/SiO$_2$ interfaces. Interfacial sliding potential energy surfaces (ISPES) are computed to determine the load-dependent shear strength and minimal-scale sliding (MSS) friction. Both quantities exhibit linear dependence on normal pressure below 3 GPa, and have non-zero values at zero pressure. Incorporating these parameters, we extend the classical Mindlin model by including adhesion and nanoscale load effects, allowing us to describe the stick to slip transition under realistic Hertzian stress distributions. The model shows that nonuniform pressure distributions substantially lower the effective static friction, and oscillatory-shear experiments on graphene-passivated contacts reproduce both the predicted stiffness-collapse signature and, in the passivated limit, the adhesion-limited shear strength obtained from simulation, supporting the model's relevance to real micro-asperity tribology.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel dual spectral-domain neural network that predicts the optical scattering T-matrix for complex 3D particles. By encoding particle shape into spherical-harmonic coefficients and using a Transformer, it bypasses computationally intensive electromagnetic solves. This establishes an efficient, data-driven method for reusable, angle-resolved characterization of photonic materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical optics, the methodology of representing complex physical inputs (geometry) and outputs (operator) in highly structured, compact spectral bases suitable for deep learning is analogous to techniques used in quantum state representation or Hamiltonian parameterization.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is rapidly predicting optical scattering from arbitrarily shaped, complex 3D particles due to morphological variability and strong angular dependence of the response.

**Main result.** A dual spectral-domain architecture successfully learns an intrinsic relationship mapping a compact geometry spectrum directly to the full T-matrix operator, enabling reusable, angle-resolved prediction.

**Method.** The authors employ a spectral-token Transformer trained on 50,000 particles to map spherical-harmonic coefficients (morphology) to the complex T-matrix (scattering operator).

**Model / system.** The system involves electromagnetic scattering from compact irregular particles. The model uses a dual spectral representation: geometry is compressed into an ordered spectrum of spherical-harmonic coefficients, and the response is encoded by the T-matrix in a spherical-vector-wave basis.

**Key observables.** Full-angle differential scattering maps, incidence-angle scans, and the complex T-matrix itself.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Wavelength (1064 nm), number of SH coefficients (e.g., 256), and generalization performance metrics like $R^2$ ($\approx 0.97$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The geometry can be sufficiently represented by a truncated spherical-harmonic spectrum, and the scattering physics can be captured by learning the T-matrix operator directly.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow from morphology encoding to T-matrix computation; one figure shows the Transformer architecture mapping spectral tokens to $	ext{Re}(\mathbf{T})$ and $	ext{Im}(\mathbf{T})$; another validates full-angle scattering maps across incidence scans.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the dual spectral model, details the training process using a spectral-token Transformer on ground-truth T-matrices derived from boundary element methods, demonstrates prediction accuracy for various angles/polarizations, and tests generalization to out-of-distribution shapes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Rapid prediction of optical scattering from arbitrarily shaped three-dimensional particles is important for particle optics and photonic characterization, but remains challenging because of the large variability of complex morphologies and the strong angular dependence of their scattering responses. To address both issues, a dual spectral-domain neural scattering model is introduced in which morphology and scattering are represented in physically ordered bases: particle geometry is compressed into only 256 spherical-harmonic coefficients, and the optical response is encoded by the complex T-matrix in a spherical-vector-wave basis. The morphology spectrum replaces high-dimensional Euclidean geometry representations, such as voxel grids, point clouds, or meshes, with a compact ordered descriptor, while the T-matrix represents a geometry-determined scattering operator that can be queried for different incidence directions, polarizations, and observation angles. A spectral-token Transformer trained on 50{,}000 irregular particles at 1064~nm maps the morphology spectrum directly to the T-matrix. The predicted operators recover modal structure and reproduce full-angle differential scattering maps and incidence-angle scans. Generalization to out-of-distribution synthetic shapes and natural sand-particle morphologies shows that the dual spectral architecture learns an intrinsic relation from the geometry spectrum to multipolar scattering. This establishes spectral-domain operator learning as a compact route for reusable, angle- and polarization-resolved optical scattering prediction of complex 3D particles.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses muon-spin rotation ($\mu$SR) to compare the mixed-state linewidths of two superconducting domes in iron pnictides. The key finding is that while one dome (SC1) shows expected field behavior, the other (SC2) exhibits an anomalous local maximum. This anomaly points toward a distinct electronic mechanism in SC2, specifically enhanced Pauli-paramagnetic effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** The comparison between two distinct superconducting domes in the same material family provides an excellent platform to study how subtle changes in electronic structure (doping/substitution) can lead to fundamentally different magnetic responses, which is relevant to understanding complex many-body physics near quantum critical points.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the anomalous field evolution of the mixed-state linewidth in two distinct superconducting domes (SC1 and SC2) within the $	ext{LaFeAsO}_{1-x}M_x$ family.

**Main result.** While SC1 shows conventional monotonic field dependence, SC2 exhibits a pronounced local maximum near 3 T at 4 K, suggesting an additional field-induced contribution from enhanced Pauli-paramagnetic effects absent in SC1.

**Method.** Transverse-field muon-spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR) measurements were used to probe the internal-field distribution in the mixed state of iron pnictides.

**Model / system.** The system is based on layered iron-based superconductors, comparing $	ext{LaFeAsO}_{0.89}	ext{F}_{0.11}$ (SC1) and $	ext{LaFeAsO}_{0.75}	ext{H}_{0.25}$ (SC2). The analysis compares the superconducting linewidth ($\sigma_{sc}$) derived from $\mu$SR data.

**Key observables.** Mixed-state linewidth ($\sigma_{sc}(T, H)$), normal-state linewidth ($\sigma_n(H)$), and the field position of local maxima ($H_{\sigma,\max}(T)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature (4 K), magnetic field (up to 8 T), doping concentrations ($x_{	ext{F}}=0.11$ vs $x_{	ext{H}}=0.25$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The anomalous behavior in SC2 is attributed to an additional field-induced contribution associated with enhanced Pauli-paramagnetic effects, which differs fundamentally from the physics governing SC1.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram of the superconducting domes and show temperature/field dependence plots ($\sigma(T)$ vs $H$) for both samples, highlighting the distinct low-temperature field behaviors.

**Paper structure.** The paper analyzes $\mu$SR data to compare SC1 and SC2. It first establishes the normal-state background, then isolates $\sigma_{sc}$. The core of the work compares the field dependence: monotonic decrease for SC1 versus nonmonotonic behavior with a local maximum for SC2.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We report a transverse-field muon-spin rotation/relaxation ($μ$SR) study of the internal-field distribution in the mixed state of LaFeAsO$_{0.89}$F$_{0.11}$ and LaFeAsO$_{0.75}$H$_{0.25}$, representative of the first (SC1) and second (SC2) superconducting domes of the LaFeAsO$_{1-x}M_x$ ($M={\rm F,H}$) family, respectively. Below the superconducting transition temperature $T_{\rm c}$, the linewidth of the internal-field distribution increases in both samples, indicating the formation of a vortex lattice. Above $T_{\rm c}$, the linewidth remains field dependent and increases approximately linearly with field, consistent with broadening of the powder spectrum caused by an anisotropic Knight shift. After subtraction of this normal-state contribution, the superconducting linewidth $σ_{\rm sc}$ exhibits qualitatively different field dependences in the two samples. At 4K, the SC1 ($x_{\rm F}=0.11$) sample shows the expected monotonic decrease with increasing field, whereas the SC2 ($x_{\rm H}=0.25$) sample develops a pronounced local maximum near 3T. A contour representation of $σ_{\rm sc}(T,H)$ further reveals a ridge of local maxima whose field position, $H_{σ,\max}(T)$, shifts to lower fields upon warming and disappears near $T_{\rm c}$. The anomalous field evolution observed in the SC2 sample is consistent with an additional field-induced contribution associated with enhanced Pauli-paramagnetic effects, highlighting the distinct electronic character of the two superconducting domes.

</details>

**Summary.** This research investigates the source of superconductivity in twisted TMD moiré semiconductors by calculating the electron-phonon coupling (EPC). The authors introduce an 'interference selection rule' based on lattice reconstruction patterns, showing that only specific phonon modes couple strongly. This mechanism points to a substantial and potentially dominant role for phonons in mediating pairing at large twist angles where superconductivity is observed.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a concrete mechanism—lattice reconstruction interference—that selects which vibrational modes couple strongly to electrons, offering a powerful diagnostic tool for understanding pairing mechanisms beyond simple continuum models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central question is determining whether superconductivity in moiré semiconductors is driven by electronic correlations, phonons, or both, which requires calculating the electron–phonon coupling (EPC).

**Main result.** A lattice reconstruction interference mechanism was discovered where phonon modes whose displacement texture matches the static lattice-reconstruction pattern couple strongly, suggesting a potentially dominant phonon contribution to superconductivity at large twist angles.

**Method.** The study combines filling-dependent Raman spectroscopy with machine-learning first-principles calculations to calculate EPC mode by mode in large supercells.

**Model / system.** The system involves moiré superlattices formed from twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) like t-WSe2 and t-MoTe2, which exhibit distinct lattice reconstruction patterns (MM, MX, XM domains).

**Key observables.** EPC strength ($\lambda$), Raman-active moiré phonon frequencies, the pattern-matching parameter $\chi$, and the total EPC constant $\lambda$ peaking near $7.34^\circ$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Twist angles (e.g., $1.89^\circ$ to $13^\circ$), carrier filling ($
u$), and the lattice reconstruction pattern.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that simple frequency shifts are insufficient, necessitating a full first-principles account incorporating intricate lattice reconstruction patterns for accurate EPC quantification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Raman spectroscopy results showing peak shifts vs. filling; they also map mode-resolved EPC strength and show the twist-angle dependence of $\lambda$, confirming its maximum near the superconducting regime.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem (superconductivity mechanism) by detailing advanced experimental measurements (Raman) alongside complex computational modeling (MLFFs). It then develops a theoretical framework using an interference selection rule ($\chi$) to calculate mode-resolved EPC, culminating in the identification of phonon dominance at specific twist angles.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Superconductivity was recently observed in twisted WSe2 and MoTe2, raising a central question: is the pairing driven by electronic correlations, by phonons, or by both? Answering it requires determining the electron-phonon coupling (EPC) in these moiré semiconductors, whose calculation in realistic supercells of thousands of atoms lies beyond the reach of direct first-principles methods. Here we combine filling-dependent Raman spectroscopy with machine-learning first-principles calculations to obtain the EPC mode by mode in supercells of up to tens of thousands of atoms. Raman reveals only a few moiré phonons whose frequencies shift strongly with filling; we trace this to an interference selection rule: a phonon couples strongly only when its displacement texture matches the static lattice-reconstruction pattern, and is otherwise suppressed by destructive interference. The rule selects the low- and high-frequency breathing modes seen in Raman and makes the coupling peak at large twist angles, near those at which superconductivity appears. Lattice-reconstruction interference thus emerges as an organizing principle for moiré EPC, pointing to a substantial, potentially dominant, phonon contribution to large-angle pairing.

</details>

**Summary.** The study reports on synthesizing and characterizing superconducting $	ext{Nd}_{1-x}	ext{Eu}_x	ext{NiO}_2$ thin films using PLD. Key findings include establishing a wide superconducting dome with high $T_c$ values and demonstrating field-enhanced superconductivity in both underdoped and overdoped regions. This work provides crucial experimental evidence regarding the role of magnetic rare-earth ions in these exotic correlated superconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work explores unconventional superconductivity in nickelates, a class of materials highly relevant to strongly correlated electron physics, which often shares theoretical links with high-Tc cuprates studied in AMO/condensed matter theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the superconducting dome formation, field-enhanced superconductivity, and re-entrant behavior in infinite-layer nickelates ($	ext{Nd}_{1-x}	ext{Eu}_x	ext{NiO}_2$).

**Main result.** PLD synthesis successfully produced high-quality films exhibiting a wide superconducting dome with an optimal $T_c \approx 31$ K, and the system displays robust field enhancement in both underdoped and overdoped regimes.

**Method.** The research employed Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) for film synthesis, followed by electrical transport measurements including resistivity ($ho(T)$), Hall effect ($R_H$), and upper critical field ($\mu_0 H_{c2}$).

**Model / system.** The physical system is the infinite-layer nickelate $	ext{Nd}_{1-x}	ext{Eu}_x	ext{NiO}_2$ thin film, where superconductivity is modulated by Eu doping ($x$). The properties are linked to the magnetic rare-earth Eu$^{2+}$ ions.

**Key observables.** Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), superconducting dome width (doping dependence), field enhancement magnitude, and nonlinear Hall resistance ($\Delta R_{xy}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping concentration $x$ ($0.2 \le x \le 0.5$), magnetic field strength (up to 35.6 T), and temperature range.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The observed field enhancement suggests mechanisms beyond the simple Jaccarino-Peter effect, and nonlinear Hall response is attributed to magnetic impurity scattering.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate XRD confirming lattice changes with doping, $ho(T)$ showing superconducting transitions across the dome, and magnetotransport data detailing $H_{c2}$ kinks and re-entrant behavior in various doping regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper details synthesis via PLD/reduction, presents transport measurements ($ho$, Hall), analyzes the doping dependence of $T_c$ (the superconducting dome), and investigates field effects to characterize the underlying pairing mechanism.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We report on the synthesis of infinite-layer Nd1-xEuxNiO2 (0<x<0.7) thin films using pulsed laser deposition (PLD) followed by topotactic reduction with CaH2. Resistivity measurements on these films reveal a superconducting dome within the doping range 0.2<x<0.5, which is wider than that achieved by molecular beam epitaxy and comparable to that obtained by chemical synthesis. The x=0.3 PLD film exhibits the optimal superconducting transition temperature Tc~31 K, much higher than those grown by other vacuum epitaxial techniques. This result indicates that PLD is an ideal approach for fabricating high-quality, high-Tc Nd1-xEuxNiO2 superconducting films. Magneto-transport measurements reveal robust field-enhanced and re-entrant superconductivity in both underdoped and overdoped regimes. At low temperatures just above the onset Tc, the Hall resistance exhibits nonlinear behavior, which may originate from magnetic impurity scattering. These results highlight the crucial role of magnetic rare-earth Eu2+ ions in producing the exotic physical properties of the infinite-layer nickelates.

</details>
